# Rendering Implementation

Also called: Gaussian Splatting Rasterization Pipeline, 3DGS Rendering

## Overview
Rendering Implementation defines the computational pipeline that transforms a learned scene representation of $M$ 3D Gaussians into a 2D image. It solves the problem of efficiently evaluating the [volume rendering equation](#2098-volume-rendering-equation.md) by projecting 3D Gaussians to 2D screen-space ellipses and [compositing](#2436-compositing.md) them via [alpha blending](#5750-alpha-blending.md) [S2, S3, unofficial]. It differs from its siblings by providing the core differentiable kernel that bridges the 3D scene representation and the 2D image plane, whereas methods like [Optimal Gaussian Splatting](3293-optimal-gaussian-splatting.md) focus on [training efficiency](#9264-optimization-and-training-efficiency.md) and [Hybrid Transparency](3294-hybrid-transparency.md) on specific blending artifacts [S2, unofficial].

## Shared principles
All rendering implementations in this family share the following mathematical and procedural core:

1.  **3D to 2D Covariance Projection**: The 3D covariance $\Sigma_{3D}$ is transformed to camera space $\Sigma'$ and then projected to 2D screen space $\Sigma_{2D}$ using a local affine approximation of the projective transformation. The Jacobian $J$ of the projection function $\phi(\mathbf{x}') = \mathbf{x}' (\mathbf{x}_0^\top \mathbf{x}')^{-1}$ is evaluated at the camera-space mean $\mu'$ [S2]. The 2D covariance is computed as:
    $$ \Sigma_{2D} = J \Sigma' J^T $$
    The matrix $J$ has rank 2. The inverse of $\Sigma_{2D}$ is effectively the inverse of the $2 \times 2$ covariance matrix obtained by skipping the third row and column of the full projected covariance [S2].

2.  **Conic Representation**: To avoid repeated matrix inversions during rasterization, the inverse 2D covariance $\Sigma_{2D}^{-1}$ is precomputed and stored as a "conic" vector containing the upper triangle elements: $[\Sigma_{2D}^{-1}[0,0], \Sigma_{2D}^{-1}[0,1], \Sigma_{2D}^{-1}[1,1]]$ [S1, unofficial].

3.  **Bounding Box Calculation**: The spatial extent of each Gaussian is determined by the 3-sigma rule. The bounding box size in pixels is derived from the diagonal elements of $\Sigma_{2D}$:
    $$ \text{bboxsize\_cam} = [3.0 \sqrt{\Sigma_{2D}[0,0]}, 3.0 \sqrt{\Sigma_{2D}[1,1]}] $$
    This is converted to screen coordinates to define the rasterization region [S1, unofficial].

4.  **Alpha Blending**: Pixels within the bounding box evaluate the 2D Gaussian value $G_{2D}$ and composite it using [front-to-back alpha blending](#1141-front-to-back-compositing-unpremultiplied.md). The weight for the $i$-th Gaussian is $w_i = \alpha_i T_i$, where $\alpha_i$ is the Gaussian's opacity modulated by $G_{2D}$ and $T_i = \prod_{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha_j)$ is the transmittance [S2, unofficial].

## Subtopics

### [3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (CPU-Sorted, Instanced)](2058-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-cpu-sorted-instanced.md)
Renders by sorting splats by camera-space depth on the [CPU](#10688-naive-sdf-generation-cpu.md) and using [hardware instancing](#3152-webgl-2-hardware-instancing.md) with [standard alpha blending](#5697-hardware-alpha-blending-compositing.md). Choose this for simpler implementation on standard graphics APIs (OpenGL/WebGL) without custom [CUDA](#3671-dual-contouring-2d-cuda.md) kernels. It is less efficient for large scenes than tile-based GPU approaches.

### [3D Gaussian Splatting Rendering (Software)](2805-3d-gaussian-splatting-rendering-software.md)
A foundational software reference that projects Gaussians using a local affine approximation and rasterizes ellipses directly. Choose this for debugging, educational purposes, or environments lacking GPU [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md). It lacks the optimizations of production renderers like [spherical harmonics evaluation](#3848-spherical-harmonics-evaluation.md) or [adaptive density control](#9188-adaptive-density-control.md).

### [3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization](2812-3d-gaussian-splatting-rasterization.md)
Provides the core differentiable kernel for real-time, photorealistic rendering using [tile-based rasterization](#5910-tile-based-rasterization.md). Choose this for production-grade training and inference where performance and differentiability are critical. It bridges the 3D representation to the 2D image plane efficiently.

## Background
The rendering pipeline for 3D [Gaussian Splatting](#946-gaussian-splatting.md) was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023 [S2]. It was developed to overcome the computational cost of evaluating the volume rendering equation via quadrature, which requires querying points outside Gaussian supports. The method uses volume [splatting](#23-splatting.md) for efficient rasterization, analogous to triangle rasterization but using Gaussians [S3, unofficial]. It is widely used in real-time novel view synthesis and 3D scene reconstruction [S2].
